stem: Which of these sorting algorithms is stable in its standard array implementation, so equal keys keep their original relative order?

options.text: Heap sort
options.why: Moving the root to the end of the array jumps equal keys past each other, so heap sort is not stable.

options.text: Merge sort
options.why: When the merge step takes from the left half on ties, equal keys keep their original order.

options.text: Quicksort
options.why: Partitioning swaps elements across long distances, so equal keys can be reordered.

options.text: Selection sort
options.why: Swapping the minimum into place can move an equal key behind its twin, e.g. [2a, 2b, 1].

explanation: Stability means records with equal keys come out in the order they went in. Merge sort is stable as long as the merge prefers the left run on ties. Heap sort, typical quicksort and array selection sort all make long-distance swaps that can reorder equal keys.

stem: Binary search only gives correct results if the array is sorted by the same ordering the search compares with.

options.text: True
options.why: Each step discards half the range by assuming everything on one side is smaller; that only holds in sorted order.

options.text: False
options.why: On unsorted data the discarded half may contain the target, so the search can miss it.

explanation: Binary search relies on the invariant that if `a[mid] < target` then every element left of mid is also smaller than the target. Without sorted order that invariant is false and the search silently returns wrong answers.

stem:
What does this return? Type a number.

```python
import bisect
bisect.bisect_left([1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 7], 4)
```
explanation: `bisect_left` returns the leftmost position where 4 could be inserted while keeping the list sorted, which is the index of the first 4: index 2. `bisect_right` would return 5, just past the last 4.

stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search over an unsorted list of n items?

options.why: Only the best case (target in the first slot) is constant time.

options.text: O(log n)
options.why: Logarithmic search needs sorted data and halving; linear search checks items one by one.

options.text: O(n)
options.why: If the target is last or absent, every one of the n items is compared.

options.text: O(n log n)
options.why: That is the cost of sorting first, not of a single linear scan.

explanation: Linear search compares items in order until it finds the target. In the worst case (last position or not present) it checks all n items, so it is O(n). It works on unsorted data, which is its advantage over binary search.

stem: Match each algorithm and situation with its running time.

options.text: O(n log n) in the worst case
options.why: Guaranteed by divide-and-conquer with balanced halves.

options.text: O(n²) in the worst case
options.why: Happens when partitions are maximally unbalanced.

options.text: O(n) in the best case
options.why: Linear time when no element needs to move.

options.text: O(n + k) for keys in 0..k
options.why: Counting work proportional to items plus key range.

prompts.text: Quicksort that always picks the last element as pivot, on already sorted input
Insertion sort on an already sorted array
Counting sort on integers in a small range

explanation: Merge sort always splits in half, so it is O(n log n) regardless of input. Last-element-pivot quicksort on sorted input produces partitions of size n−1 and 0, giving O(n²). Insertion sort on sorted input makes one comparison per element. Counting sort tallies keys and does O(n + k) work without comparisons.

stem: Which algorithm do Python's `sorted()` and `list.sort()` use?

options.text: Timsort, a stable hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort
options.why: CPython has used Timsort (with run detection and galloping merges) since 2.3.

options.text: Introsort, a quicksort that falls back to heap sort when recursion gets deep
options.why: That is what C++ std::sort typically uses; it is not stable.

options.text: Heap sort, chosen because it needs only O(1) auxiliary memory
options.why: Heap sort is unstable, and Python guarantees a stable sort.

options.text: Radix sort on the binary representation of the keys
options.why: Python sorts arbitrary comparable objects, which rules out a digit-based sort.

explanation: CPython's list sort is Timsort: it finds already-ordered runs, extends short runs with binary insertion sort and merges them with a galloping merge. It is stable and runs in O(n) on input that is already sorted. (CPython 3.11 switched its merge policy to powersort, but it is still a stable Timsort-style merge sort.)

stem: One outer pass of bubble sort compares each adjacent pair from left to right and swaps it if it is out of order. What is the list after one pass over `[5, 1, 4, 2, 8]`?

options.why: That stops after the first swap; a pass continues through every adjacent pair.
The 5 bubbles right past 1, 4 and 2, then stops before the larger 8.
That is the fully sorted result, which needs a second pass here.
The 5 is compared with the 2 as well, so it moves one place further.

explanation: Pass trace: (5,1) swap → [1,5,4,2,8]; (5,4) swap → [1,4,5,2,8]; (5,2) swap → [1,4,2,5,8]; (5,8) no swap. After one pass the largest element is guaranteed to be at the end, but the rest is not yet sorted.

stem: Selection sort makes about n²/2 comparisons even when the input is already sorted.

options.text: True
options.why: It always scans the whole unsorted suffix to find the minimum, whatever the order.

options.text: False
options.why: Unlike insertion sort, selection sort cannot stop early on sorted input.

explanation: Selection sort scans the remaining n−1, n−2, … elements to find each minimum, so it always makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons. That is 499,500 comparisons for 1,000 already-sorted items, while insertion sort needs only 999.

stem: Insertion sort runs on `[4, 3, 2, 10, 12, 1, 5, 6]`. What does the array look like after the outer loop has finished processing indexes 1 and 2?

options.why: That is the state after index 1 only; index 2 still has to be inserted.
After two insertions the first three slots hold the sorted prefix 2, 3, 4.
The 1 is not touched until the loop reaches index 5.
Insertion shifts all larger elements, so 3 and 4 both move right of the 2.

explanation: Insertion sort keeps a sorted prefix. Index 1 inserts 3 before 4 → [3,4,2,…]. Index 2 inserts 2 before both → [2,3,4,10,12,1,5,6]. The rest of the array is unchanged until later iterations.

stem: Which of these sorting algorithms are stable in their standard array form? (Choose two.)

options.text: Insertion sort
options.why: It only shifts strictly larger elements, so an equal key never passes its twin.

options.text: Merge sort
options.why: Taking from the left run on ties preserves the original order of equal keys.

options.text: Heap sort
options.why: Building and draining the heap moves equal keys past each other.

options.text: Selection sort with swaps
options.why: Swapping the minimum forward can jump an equal key over its twin.

options.text: Quicksort with Lomuto partitioning
options.why: Partition swaps are long-distance and reorder equal keys.

explanation: Insertion sort and merge sort are stable because elements only move past strictly greater (or, for merge, strictly smaller) keys. Heap sort, swap-based selection sort and quicksort move elements across long distances, so they can reorder equal keys.

stem:
How many times does 4 appear, computed with the `bisect` module?

```python
import bisect
a = [1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 7]
print(bisect.bisect_right(a, 4) - bisect.bisect_left(a, 4))
```

options.why: That would mean bisect_right points at the last 4 rather than just past it.
bisect_right is 5 and bisect_left is 2, and the difference counts the equal run.
That is bisect_right on its own, not the count.
That is the length of the list, not the number of 4s.

explanation: `bisect_left` gives the index of the first 4 (2) and `bisect_right` gives the index just past the last 4 (5). Their difference, 3, is the number of 4s, found in O(log n) instead of a linear scan.

stem: What extra memory does a standard top-down merge sort of an array need?

options.text: O(1), because the merge step can always work in place
options.why: Simple in-place merging of arrays is O(n²) or very complex; standard merge sort uses a buffer.

options.text: O(log n), the same as the recursion stack
options.why: The stack is O(log n), but the merge buffer dominates.

options.text: O(n) for the merge buffer plus the O(log n) stack
options.why: Merging two runs needs a temporary array as large as the input.

options.text: O(n log n), one buffer per recursion level kept alive
options.why: Buffers are reused or freed level by level, so they never all coexist.

explanation: Merging two sorted runs into one requires a temporary array, so merge sort on arrays uses Θ(n) auxiliary space. The recursion adds O(log n) stack frames. This extra memory is the main reason quicksort or heap sort is preferred when memory is tight.

stem: A quicksort always picks the last element as its pivot. Why does it take quadratic time on an already sorted array?

options.text: Because every element must be swapped with the pivot during each partition
options.why: On sorted input the elements are already left of the pivot; the cost is in the comparisons.

options.text: Each partition splits n items into n−1 and 0, so recursion goes n levels deep
options.why: The pivot is the maximum each time, so each level removes only one element.

options.text: Because sorted input forces a fallback to bubble sort in most implementations
options.why: Plain quicksort has no such fallback; the degradation comes from the pivot choice.

options.text: Because the recursion stack overflows and restarts the sort from the beginning
options.why: Deep recursion can overflow, but sorting never restarts; the work itself is n²/2 comparisons.

explanation: With the last element as pivot on sorted input, every pivot is the largest remaining value. Partitioning makes n−1, n−2, … comparisons and leaves an empty right side, so the total is about n²/2 and the recursion is n levels deep (499 levels for 500 items in a test run). Random or median-of-three pivots avoid this.

stem: Put the steps of the standard "merge overlapping intervals" algorithm in order.

options.text: Sort the intervals by their start value
options.why: Sorting puts every overlap next to its partner.

options.text: Start the output list with the first interval
options.why: The first sorted interval opens the first merged block.

options.text: For each next interval, compare its start with the end of the last output interval
options.why: Only the last merged block can overlap the current interval.

options.text: If it overlaps, extend the last end to the larger of the two ends; otherwise append it
options.why: Taking the max handles intervals nested inside the current block.

explanation: Sorting by start (O(n log n)) guarantees that any interval overlapping the current block comes right after it. A single linear scan then either extends the last block (using max of the two ends) or starts a new one.

options.why: That is what you get without max(): [2,3] would shrink the block to end at 3.
[2,3] lies inside [1,4], [4,6] touches it (4 <= 4), and [8,9] starts a new block.
With `<=`, intervals that share an endpoint are merged.
[8,9] starts after 6, so it is not merged with the earlier block.

explanation: Trace: [1,4]; [2,3] overlaps → end stays max(4,3)=4; [4,6] overlaps because 4 <= 4 → end becomes 6; [8,9] starts after 6 → new block. Result [[1,6],[8,9]]. Using `out[-1][1] = e` instead of max() is a classic bug that gives [[1,3],[4,6],[8,9]].

stem: A sorted array holds 1,000,000 distinct values. In the worst case, how many elements does a standard binary search compare against before it finds the target or reports it absent? Type a number.
explanation: Each comparison halves the remaining range. The worst case needs ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 probes: ⌊log₂ 1,000,000⌋ = 19, so 20 probes. That is why binary search over a million items is near-instant, while linear search may need a million comparisons.

stem: You must sort the ages (0–120) of 10 million users. Which approach is asymptotically fastest?

options.text: Merge sort, because O(n log n) is optimal for sorting
options.why: n log n is optimal only for comparison sorts; small integer keys allow linear time.

options.text: Counting sort, O(n + k) with k = 121 possible values
options.why: Tally each age, then emit them in order: linear time in n.

options.text: Quicksort, because it is fastest in practice on large arrays
options.why: It still needs about n log n comparisons, while counting sort needs none.

options.text: Binary insertion sort, because binary search makes each insert O(log n)
options.why: Finding the slot is O(log n), but shifting elements makes each insert O(n).

explanation: The Ω(n log n) lower bound applies to comparison sorts. With integer keys in a small range (k = 121), counting sort counts occurrences and rebuilds the output in O(n + k), which is effectively O(n) for 10 million items.

stem: Which statements about heap sort are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Its worst-case running time is O(n log n)
options.why: Building the heap is O(n) and each of the n extractions costs O(log n).

options.text: It sorts in place, with O(1) extra memory
options.why: The heap lives inside the array being sorted.

options.text: It is stable, because heap order respects insertion order
options.why: Swapping the root to the end reorders equal keys, so it is unstable.

options.text: It runs in O(n) on input that is already sorted
options.why: It still builds a heap and extracts n times, about n log n work on any input.

options.text: It usually beats quicksort because of its cache locality
options.why: Sift-down jumps between distant indexes, so its cache behaviour is worse than quicksort's.

explanation: Heap sort guarantees O(n log n) in the worst case and needs only O(1) extra memory, but it is not stable, not adaptive to sorted input, and its scattered memory access usually makes it slower than quicksort in practice.

stem: Python's `sorted()` makes only n − 1 comparisons when the input list is already in ascending order.

options.text: True
options.why: Timsort detects the whole list as one ascending run and has nothing to merge.

options.text: False
options.why: Timsort is adaptive; it does not perform n log n comparisons on presorted input.

explanation: Timsort first scans for natural runs. An already-sorted list is a single run, found with n − 1 comparisons, and no merging is needed. Counting comparisons with a custom `__lt__` on `sorted(range(1000))` shows exactly 999.
reference: Python docs: Sorting Techniques; CPython listsort.txt

stem:
What does this print?

```python
rows = [("Cara", "Eng"), ("Abe", "Ops"), ("Bo", "Eng"), ("Ann", "Ops")]
rows = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r[0])   # by name
rows = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r[1])   # then by department
print(rows)
```

options.text: `[('Cara', 'Eng'), ('Bo', 'Eng'), ('Abe', 'Ops'), ('Ann', 'Ops')]`
options.why: That keeps the original order within each department, ignoring the first sort.

options.text: `[('Bo', 'Eng'), ('Cara', 'Eng'), ('Abe', 'Ops'), ('Ann', 'Ops')]`
options.why: The stable second sort keeps the name order inside each department.

options.text: `[('Abe', 'Ops'), ('Ann', 'Ops'), ('Bo', 'Eng'), ('Cara', 'Eng')]`
options.why: That is the name order only; the second sort groups by department.

options.text: The order within each department is unspecified
options.why: Python guarantees a stable sort, so ties keep their previous order.

explanation: Because Python's sort is stable, sorting by the secondary key (name) and then by the primary key (department) produces department order with names sorted inside each department. This "sort by least significant key first" trick is how multi-key sorts and LSD radix sort work.

stem: A matrix has each row sorted, and every row starts with a value larger than the last value of the row above. What is the best way to search it for a value?

options.text: Binary search each row in turn, for O(m log n) total over all rows
options.why: That ignores the ordering between rows, which makes the whole matrix one sorted list.

options.text: One binary search over indexes 0..m·n−1 using (i // n, i % n)
options.why: The matrix read row by row is one sorted sequence, so one search costs O(log(mn)).

options.text: Start at the top-right corner and step left or down, for O(m + n)
options.why: That works for matrices sorted only by row and column, but it is slower than needed here.

options.text: Flatten into a hash set first, then look each value up in O(1)
options.why: Building the set costs O(mn), far more than a single search.

explanation: With rows sorted and each row starting above the previous row's end, reading the matrix row by row gives one sorted array of length mn. A single binary search with index mapping (i // n, i % n) finds any value in O(log(mn)). The staircase walk from the top-right corner is the right tool for the weaker "rows and columns sorted" matrix.

options.text: It returns 1
options.why: That is the intended answer, but the loop never reaches it.

options.text: It returns 0
options.why: The loop never exits, so nothing is returned.

options.text: It loops forever
options.why: With lo = 0 and hi = 1, mid is 0 and lo = mid never changes the range.

options.text: It raises IndexError
options.why: All indexes stay within 0..1, so no lookup goes out of range.

explanation: When hi = lo + 1, floor division makes mid = lo. If `a[mid] <= t`, then `lo = mid` leaves the range unchanged, so the loop spins forever (also for t = 1). Whenever a branch sets `lo = mid`, use the upper middle `mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2` so the range always shrinks; with that fix f([1, 2], 2) returns 1.

stem:
In search-in-rotated-sorted-array, the code decides which half is sorted. Why must the test be `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` rather than `nums[lo] < nums[mid]`?

```python
if nums[lo] <= nums[mid]:     # left half sorted
    if nums[lo] <= t < nums[mid]: hi = mid - 1
    else: lo = mid + 1
else:                         # right half sorted
    if nums[mid] < t <= nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid - 1
```

options.text: With `<`, duplicate values would make a sorted left half look unsorted to the test
options.why: The problem assumes distinct values; the issue appears even without duplicates.

options.text: When lo == mid the one-element left half is sorted; `<` picks the wrong half
options.why: For [3, 1] and target 1, `<` sends the search left and returns −1.

options.text: With `<`, the loop never terminates on arrays rotated by one position
options.why: Every branch still moves lo or hi, so the loop ends; it just returns the wrong answer.

options.text: It makes no difference; the two tests are equivalent for distinct values
options.why: They differ exactly when lo == mid, which happens for two-element ranges.

explanation: When the range has two elements, mid equals lo, and a single element is trivially sorted. With `<` the test fails and the code treats the right half as sorted, so for [3, 1] searching 1 it discards the target and returns −1. With `<=` it returns 1, and an exhaustive test over all rotations of sizes 1–7 found no errors.
reference: LeetCode 33: Search in Rotated Sorted Array

stem: A quicksort is degrading to O(n²) on already sorted production data. Which pivot strategies avoid that behaviour on sorted input? (Choose two.)

options.text: Pick a uniformly random element as the pivot
options.why: No fixed input can reliably produce bad splits; expected time is O(n log n).

options.text: Use the median of the first, middle and last elements
options.why: On sorted input that median is the true middle, giving balanced splits.

options.text: Always use the first element as the pivot
options.why: On sorted input the first element is the minimum, so every split is 0 and n−1.

options.text: Always use the last element as the pivot
options.why: On sorted input the last element is the maximum, giving the same worst case.

options.text: Use the smallest of the first, middle and last elements
options.why: That deliberately picks a low pivot, which keeps the splits unbalanced.

explanation: First- or last-element pivots hit their worst case on sorted or reverse-sorted input, which is common in practice. A random pivot makes the expected time O(n log n) for every input, and median-of-three picks the exact middle of sorted data. Many library sorts add more safeguards, such as introsort's heap sort fallback.

options.why: The final swap exchanges the pivot with the 8 at index 5, so 8 ends up last.
Five smaller elements go first in scan order, then 6 swaps with the 8 at index 5.
Partitioning only splits around the pivot; it does not sort each side.
Five elements are smaller than 6, so the pivot lands at index 5.

explanation: Trace: 3 stays at 0; 8 is skipped; 2 swaps with 8 → [3,2,8,…]; 5 swaps with 8; 1 swaps with 8; 4 swaps with 8 → [3,2,5,1,4,8,7,6]; 7 is skipped. Finally the pivot 6 swaps with a[5]=8 → [3,2,5,1,4,6,7,8], returning 5. Running the code confirms this.

stem: How many inversions (pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]) does `[2, 4, 1, 3, 5]` contain? This is what a merge-sort inversion counter returns. Type a number.
explanation: The inversions are (2,1), (4,1) and (4,3), so the count is 3. Merge sort counts them in O(n log n): whenever an element from the right half is merged before elements still left in the left half, it adds that many inversions.

stem: You need the median of 10 million unsorted numbers once. Which approach gives the best expected running time?

options.text: Sort the numbers, then index the middle, for O(n log n)
options.why: Correct, but sorting does far more work than selecting one order statistic.

options.text: Quickselect with a random pivot, O(n) expected
options.why: It recurses into only one side of each partition, so the work shrinks geometrically.

options.text: Push everything into a min-heap and pop n/2 times, O(n) total
options.why: Each pop costs O(log n), so n/2 pops cost O(n log n).

options.text: Quickselect, because it is O(n) even in the worst case
options.why: Plain quickselect is O(n²) in the worst case; only median-of-medians guarantees O(n).

explanation: Quickselect partitions like quicksort but recurses only into the side containing the kth element. With random pivots the expected work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … = O(n). Its worst case is O(n²), which median-of-medians pivoting avoids at the cost of larger constants.

stem: Packages with weights 1, 2, …, 10 (in that order) must be shipped within 5 days. Each day the ship takes a prefix of the remaining packages without exceeding its capacity. Binary search on the answer finds the minimum capacity. What is it?

options.why: Capacity 10 needs more than 5 days, because 9 and 10 each need a day of their own.
Days [1..5], [6,7], [8], [9], [10] fit in exactly 5 days.
Capacity 11 needs 7 days; the feasibility check fails until 15.
That ships everything in one day; it is the upper bound of the search, not the minimum.

explanation: Search capacities between max(weights) = 10 and sum(weights) = 55. A capacity is feasible if greedily filling each day uses at most 5 days, and feasibility is monotonic, so binary search applies. 14 needs 6 days; 15 gives [1–5]=15, [6,7]=13, [8], [9], [10] in 5 days. Running the code returns 15.
reference: LeetCode 1011: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days

stem: Koko eats bananas from piles `[3, 6, 7, 11]` at k bananas per hour; each hour she eats from one pile only (a partial pile still takes the full hour). What is the minimum integer k that lets her finish within 8 hours? Type a number.
explanation: Hours at speed k are Σ ceil(pile / k). At k = 3: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 hours (too slow). At k = 4: 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 hours. Since hours only decrease as k grows, binary searching k in [1, max(pile)] finds 4.

stem: Keeping a Python list sorted with `bisect.insort` costs O(log n) per insertion.

options.text: True
options.why: Only finding the position is logarithmic; inserting into the list still shifts elements.

options.text: False
options.why: insort finds the slot with binary search, but list.insert shifts later elements, which is O(n).

explanation: `insort` does an O(log n) binary search and then `list.insert`, which moves every element after the slot. Each insertion is therefore O(n), and n insertions are O(n²). For many inserts, use a balanced tree, a heap, or sort once at the end.

stem: Match each problem with the technique that fits it best.

options.text: Binary search on the answer
options.why: Search a monotonic yes/no predicate over possible answers.

options.text: Quickselect
options.why: Partition and recurse into one side to find the kth element.

options.text: Sort by start, then sweep
options.why: Ordering makes overlaps adjacent for one linear pass.

options.text: Cyclic sort
options.why: Place each value v at index v−1 by swapping.

prompts.text: Smallest ship capacity that delivers all packages within D days
Third-largest value in an unsorted array, needed once
Find the missing number in an array holding 1..n with one value gone, using O(1) extra space

explanation: Monotonic feasibility questions ("can we do it with capacity c?") suggest binary search on the answer. One-off order statistics suggest quickselect. Overlap problems become linear after sorting by start. Arrays holding a permutation of 1..n can be fixed in place by cyclic sort, after which the first mismatched index reveals the missing value.

options.why: [0,10] and [5,15] overlap, so at least two rooms are needed.
[5,15] needs a second room; [10,20] reuses the room that frees up at 10.
The meeting ending at 10 frees its room exactly when the [10,20] meeting starts.
The heap always holds at least one end time after the first meeting.

explanation: Sorted: [0,10], [5,15], [10,20]. Room 1 takes [0,10]. [5,15] starts before 10, so room 2 opens. [10,20] starts at 10, and the earliest end is 10 ≤ 10, so it reuses that room. The heap ends with two end times, so 2 rooms are needed.

stem: Which statements about LSD (least-significant-digit-first) radix sort are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Each per-digit pass must use a stable sort, such as counting sort
options.why: Stability preserves the order established by earlier, less significant digits.

options.text: For d-digit keys in base b it runs in O(d · (n + b))
options.why: Each of the d passes is a counting sort over n items and b buckets.

options.text: It processes the most significant digit first and recurses into buckets
options.why: That describes MSD radix sort; LSD goes from the last digit to the first.

options.text: It compares pairs of keys, so it obeys the Ω(n log n) lower bound
options.why: It never compares keys, so the comparison lower bound does not apply.

options.text: It sorts arbitrary strings of different lengths without padding
options.why: LSD needs fixed-length keys; variable lengths need padding or MSD radix sort.

explanation: LSD radix sort sorts by the last digit first and finishes with the most significant digit. It works only because every pass is stable: ties on the current digit keep the order from earlier digits. With d digits in base b it costs O(d(n + b)) and makes no comparisons.

stem: You are choosing between merge sort and quicksort. Which statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Merge sort suits linked lists: it needs no random access and merges by relinking nodes
options.why: List merging needs no buffer, which removes merge sort's main drawback.

options.text: On arrays, quicksort's in-place partitioning is usually faster thanks to cache locality
options.why: Sequential scans over one array beat copying into and out of a merge buffer.

options.text: Merge sort on arrays is easily made in-place with O(1) extra memory at the same speed
options.why: In-place merging exists but is complex and much slower in practice.

options.text: Quicksort becomes stable when the partition comparison uses <= instead of <
options.why: Long-distance swaps still reorder equal keys, whichever comparison is used.

options.text: Heap sort beats both on modern CPUs because it is in place and O(n log n)
options.why: Its scattered sift-down accesses cause more cache misses than either.

explanation: Merge sort shines on linked lists (no random access, no extra buffer) and when stability or guaranteed O(n log n) matters. On arrays, quicksort's in-place partitioning and sequential memory access usually make it faster, which is why many libraries use quicksort variants for primitives and merge-based Timsort when stability is required.

stem: Each algorithm sorts the same already-sorted list of 1,000 distinct integers. Order them by the number of key comparisons they make, fewest first.

options.text: Insertion sort
options.why: One comparison per element on sorted input.

options.text: Top-down merge sort
options.why: Each merge exhausts one half after about half its length.

options.text: Heap sort
options.why: Builds a max-heap, then sifts down n times regardless of order.

options.text: Selection sort
options.why: Always scans the entire unsorted suffix.

explanation: Counting comparisons in Python on range(1000): insertion sort 999, top-down merge sort 4,932, heap sort 17,583, selection sort 499,500. Insertion sort is adaptive, merge sort does about (n/2)·log₂ n comparisons when one side always runs out first, heap sort still does ~2n log n work, and selection sort is always n(n−1)/2.
reference: Measured with instrumented implementations; Sedgewick & Wayne §2.1–2.4

stem: How does Hoare's original partition scheme differ from Lomuto's?

options.text: Hoare puts the pivot at its final sorted position, while Lomuto does not
options.why: It is the reverse: Lomuto places the pivot exactly; Hoare only splits the range.

options.text: About three times fewer swaps, but the pivot may not end at the split index
options.why: Two converging pointers swap only misplaced pairs; recursion uses [lo..p] and [p+1..hi].

options.text: Hoare is stable, which is why most standard library sorts prefer it over Lomuto
options.why: Like Lomuto, Hoare partitioning swaps across long distances and is unstable.

options.text: Hoare degrades to O(n²) on arrays of all-equal elements, while Lomuto does not
options.why: The opposite: Hoare's pointers stop on equal keys and split them evenly, while Lomuto degrades.

explanation: Hoare partitioning moves two pointers toward each other and swaps pairs that are on the wrong side, doing roughly a third of Lomuto's swaps on average. It returns a split point such that everything in [lo..p] is ≤ everything in [p+1..hi], but the pivot itself need not be at p, so the recursion includes p on the left. It also handles many duplicates far better than Lomuto.

stem: A textbook quicksort uses Lomuto partitioning (`if a[j] < pivot`) with the last element as pivot. What happens on an array of 500 identical values?

options.text: It runs in O(n), because no swaps are needed
options.why: Comparisons still happen at every level; the problem is how many levels there are.

options.text: It runs in O(n log n), because equal keys split evenly
options.why: With `<`, nothing goes left, so the split is never even.

options.text: It degrades to O(n²), with recursion about n levels deep
options.why: Each partition places only the pivot and leaves n−1 equal items in one side.

options.text: It raises an error because the partition index goes out of range
options.why: The indexes stay valid; the algorithm is just very slow.

explanation: With all keys equal, `a[j] < pivot` is never true, so each partition puts the pivot at the front and leaves n−1 items on the right. That gives n levels and about n²/2 comparisons; a test on 500 equal values reached recursion depth 499. Three-way (Dutch national flag) partitioning, which groups keys equal to the pivot, fixes this and makes all-equal input O(n).

stem: A class counts every call to its `__lt__` method. How many comparisons does `sorted()` make on a list of 1,000 such objects that are already in ascending order? Type a number.
explanation: Timsort scans for a natural run: it compares each adjacent pair once, finds that the whole list is one ascending run of length 1,000, and has nothing left to merge. That is n − 1 = 999 comparisons, which is what the counting experiment reports.
reference: CPython listsort.txt; Python docs: Sorting Techniques

stem: Any comparison sort can be modelled as a binary decision tree whose leaves are the possible orderings. What is the minimum number of comparisons any comparison sort needs in the worst case to sort 5 distinct elements?

options.why: Five comparisons give at most 32 outcomes, too few for 120 orderings.
That is the number of pairs; a good algorithm needs far fewer.
2⁷ = 128 ≥ 5! = 120, and 7 comparisons are achievable for n = 5.
2⁶ = 64 leaves cannot distinguish all 120 orderings.

explanation: A decision tree of height h has at most 2ʰ leaves, and it needs one leaf per permutation: 5! = 120. So h ≥ ⌈log₂ 120⌉ = 7. Merge insertion (Ford–Johnson) achieves 7 for five elements, so 7 is exact. In general this argument gives the Ω(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorting.

stem:
Four versions of "return the index of the first occurrence of t in a sorted list, or −1" are below. Which are correct for every input?

```python
def v1(a, t):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] < t: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid
    return lo if lo < len(a) and a[lo] == t else -1

def v2(a, t):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] == t: return mid
        if a[mid] < t: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1

def v3(a, t):
    lo, hi, ans = 0, len(a) - 1, -1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] >= t:
            if a[mid] == t: ans = mid
            hi = mid - 1
        else: lo = mid + 1
    return ans

def v4(a, t):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] < t: lo = mid
        else: hi = mid
    return lo if a and a[lo] == t else -1
```

options.text: v1 only, because the others mishandle duplicates
options.why: v3 also handles duplicates by recording a match and continuing left.

options.text: v1 and v3
options.why: v2 returns any match, not the first; v4 can loop forever because lo = mid may not move.

options.text: v1, v2 and v3
options.why: v2 stops at whichever occurrence mid hits first, e.g. index 1 in [2, 2, 2].

options.text: All four
options.why: v4 spins when a[mid] < t and hi = lo + 1, since lo = mid changes nothing.

explanation: v1 is the half-open lower_bound pattern and v3 records the latest match while continuing left; both passed an exhaustive test over all sorted arrays of length 0–6 with values 0–2. v2 is a plain membership search that returns whichever equal element mid lands on. v4 never terminates in thousands of those cases, because `lo = mid` with floor mid does not shrink a two-element range.

stem: Which statements about counting sort are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: It runs in O(n + k) for n integers in the range 0..k
options.why: One pass to count, one pass over k buckets, one pass to place items.

options.text: Placing items using prefix sums while scanning the input right to left keeps it stable
options.why: Equal keys fill their slots from the back in reverse scan order, preserving input order.

options.text: It is a comparison sort, so it cannot beat O(n log n)
options.why: It only indexes by key value and never compares two items.

options.text: It sorts arbitrary floating-point numbers directly
options.why: It needs integer keys in a bounded range to index the count array.

options.text: Its extra memory is O(1), independent of the key range
options.why: The count array alone takes O(k) memory, plus O(n) for the output.

explanation: Counting sort tallies how many times each key occurs, turns the tallies into prefix sums (final positions), and places each item. Scanning the input from the right while decrementing positions keeps equal keys in order, which is why it serves as the stable inner sort of LSD radix sort. It needs O(n + k) time and memory and is only practical when k is not much larger than n.

stem: You must sort a 100 GB log file on a machine with 8 GB of RAM. Order the steps of an external merge sort.

options.text: Read a chunk that fits in memory (about 8 GB)
options.why: The chunk size is bounded by available RAM.

options.text: Sort the chunk in memory
options.why: Any fast in-memory sort works for a single chunk.

options.text: Write the sorted chunk to disk as a run, and repeat until the input is consumed
options.why: About ⌈100 / 8⌉ = 13 sorted runs are produced.

options.text: Merge all runs with a k-way merge driven by a min-heap of each run's current head
options.why: Buffered reads from 13 runs, each pop taking O(log 13).

explanation: External sorting splits the input into memory-sized chunks, sorts each one and writes it out as a run (13 runs here). A single k-way merge then streams through all runs, keeping one buffered head per run in a min-heap. With 13 runs and enough buffer memory this finishes in one merge pass, so the data is read and written about twice in total.

stem: What does inserting `[4, 8]` into `[[1, 2], [3, 5], [6, 7], [8, 10], [12, 16]]` (non-overlapping, sorted) produce, merging where needed?

options.why: Intervals that touch at 8 are merged too, joining [3,8] with [8,10].
[4,8] overlaps [3,5], [6,7] and [8,10], which all collapse into [3,10].
That only inserts in sorted position without merging overlaps.
The merged block keeps the smaller start, 3, from [3,5].

explanation: Intervals ending before 4 ([1,2]) are copied. Every interval overlapping [4,8] — [3,5], [6,7] and [8,10] (touching at 8) — is absorbed, taking min start 3 and max end 10. The rest ([12,16]) is copied. Result [[1,2],[3,10],[12,16]], in O(n).

stem: Each row and each column of `[[1, 5, 9], [10, 11, 13], [12, 13, 15]]` is sorted. Binary searching on value (counting how many entries are ≤ mid with a staircase walk) finds the 8th smallest element. What is it?

options.why: Only 6 entries (1, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12) are ≤ 12, so the 8th is larger.
Entries ≤ 13 number 8 (13 appears twice), and fewer than 8 are ≤ 12.
15 is the 9th and largest value.
Only 5 entries are ≤ 11.

explanation: Sorted, the values are 1, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 13, 15, so the 8th smallest is 13. The binary search finds the smallest value v with count(≤ v) ≥ 8: count(12) = 6 and count(13) = 8. Each count is an O(n) staircase walk, so the search costs O(n log(max − min)).
reference: LeetCode 378: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix

options.why: Index 1 (value 2) is a peak too, but the search moves right and never returns there.
The search climbs the rising slope on the right and stops at 6.
Index 6 holds 4, which is smaller than its neighbour 6.
Index 4 holds 5, and its right neighbour 6 is larger.

explanation: Trace: lo=0, hi=6, mid=3 (3 < 5) → lo=4; mid=5 (6 > 4) → hi=5; mid=4 (5 < 6) → lo=5; stop at 5. Moving toward the larger neighbour always keeps at least one peak in range, which is why this O(log n) search works even on unsorted data. It returns some peak, not necessarily the first.
